newsitem.title: BOSNIA: OSCE appeals body urges Bosnian vote recount.
newsitem.headline: OSCE appeals body urges Bosnian vote recount.

text.p: Results of Bosnia's elections this month were cast into doubt on Friday when an election appeals group established under the Dayton peace process called for a complete recount of all votes cast.

The Election Appeals Sub-Commission of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) mission in Bosnia issued the recommendation on the basis of complaints alleging the number of votes cast in the September 14 elections was suspiciously high.
OSCE conducted the Bosnian elections under a mandate provided by last December's Dayton peace agreement, which ended 43 months of war in the country.
The Election Appeals Sub-Commission made its recommendation to the OSCE's Provisional Election Commission (PEC), the final election authority in Bosnia.
"This recount is necessary to rebut the possible inference that the high turnout reported is due to miscalculations in the count rather than fraud," the sub-commission said.
The PEC was meeting on Friday afternoon to consider the sub-commission's recommendation.
The PEC, which includes representation from Bosnia's Moslem, Serb and Croat communities, is chaired by Ambassador Robert Frowick, an American.
The group operates on the basis of consensus whenever possible, but Frowick has the final say as chairman.
A recount would involve days if not weeks of delay in certifying the final results of the complex elections.
It would also wreck plans to begin the immediate formation of the joint government institutions for which Bosnians voted under the provisions of the Dayton agreement.

Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic, a Moslem and winner of the chairmanship of Bosnia's three-man collective presidency by 41,000 votes based on preliminary final results announced by OSCE this week, could end up unseated by a recount.
The second-place finisher, Momcilo Krajisnik, a hardline Serb separatist, would likely prove unacceptable as a chairman to Bosnia's Moslems.
Plans to try to hold Bosnian municipal elections in late November might also be adversely affected.
If a recount confirmed substantial irregularities, the entire election might be voided in a huge set-back to the peace process.
The Appeals Sub-Commission decision, which cited an overall turnout rate of 77 percent for the September 14 elections, posed the following question:

"Is the...turnout figure of 77 percent, considered in the light of known obstacles to voting for certain groups of voters, so high that it raises a significant possibility of double voting, other forms of fraud or counting irregularities?"
"In the view of the Sub-Comission, it does."
The International Crisis Group (ICG), a private non-profit body which had lodged a formal complaint with the Appeals Sub- Commission, welcomed Friday's decision.
"ICG strongly urges the Provisional Election Commission to accept the (sub-commission) recommendation and order a complete and transparent recount of all the ballots cast," an ICG statement said.
"Should the recount confirm the suspiciously high voter turn-out figures then the PEC must declare the September 14 elections null and void."
